rows: Three-tier rollout, fully in by Q4
Celsius is deliberately 'backdooring' the energy category - built brand credibility and authenticity in fitness/health-and-wellness channels before pushing into traditional convenience.
Strong incrementality: 37% of the energy category's ~$100M recent growth (largest single contributor, ahead of Red Bull and Monster), with ~90% non-cannibalizing.
~4 category share (roughly doubled from ~2% over 12 months); #2 on Amazon (~8.4 share); recently passed Rockstar to become #4 energy brand, with Bang (#3) the next target.
2022 is 'really our first year in convenience' (~68,000 doors), anchored by the new Circle K rollout (~5,000 doors, ~8 flavors nationwide).
Velocity rises even as distribution expands - two simultaneous tailwinds: DSD conversion delivers a 100%+ lift, and new doors are the most productive (convenience).
April 1 frontline (list) price increase confirmed under a three-tier rollout fully in by Q4; targets a $2.59-$2.79 convenience price point (premium to Monster, below Red Bull); magnitude withheld.
Management deliberately over-investing ahead of revenue in sales and SG&A; benchmarks margin inflection against Monster's ~$700-800M revenue range.
Significant untapped distribution remains: Walgreens (not yet in), Dollar Tree, and improved Kroger beverage-set placement (currently mainly in HPC sets).
Optimization runway in existing doors - adding flavors (e.g., Walmart from 3 to 6-7) and cold/secondary placement could double or triple sales per outlet.

Shelf-space strategy: own the cooler and trade floor, displace lower-turning 'wounded gazelles', warrant double-facings for high-turning SKUs; positioning for the NACS October season and next-year resets (fighting for two shelves).
Celsius acquired Numerator to become more analytical and a category thought leader; will share Numerator data on the next earnings call.
High-continuity, loyal consumer base; business model could not work on new customers alone (acquisition is expensive on a ~$2.50 can).
Energy is highly promotional (~27-28 weeks of promotion annually); half-the-year cadence is an industry norm expected by retailers, not a proven optimum.
Brand credibility likened to Lululemon; deliberately inclusive/unisex packaging - 'something for everyone' rather than a high-aggressiveness niche.
Industry context: Bang's move to Pepsi helped catapult Celsius's distribution network; NACS-driven retailer shelf reallocation (reducing water/tea/CSD facings) creates opportunity.
How incremental is Celsius rather than sourcing from Monster/Red Bull, and does the functional-energy space coexist with legacy players?

Celsius was 37% of the category's ~$100M recent growth (~90% non-cannibalizing); brand credibility built over years in health-and-wellness channels; club expansion (Costco) fully incremental with no cannibalization.
Is the younger consumer cohort also split evenly male-female?
Yes - roughly 55-45 male-female per anecdotal data; reflects deliberately inclusive, unisex packaging.
How do retailer discussions on incremental space go - taking space from others or adding to total shelf space?

Rising velocity over 18-24 months lets Celsius educate retailers on money per slot; bought Numerator to be more analytical; grabbing share requires owning the cooler and displacing lower-turning SKUs.
Selling the incrementality argument to buyers
Given higher velocity, is winning shelf space an easy sell, and what do buyers say if they decline?

More opportunity than last year's skepticism; uses the 37% / ~90%-non-cannibalization data to argue Celsius shoppers spend more per shop; framed goal as the broader beverage and total-energy category.
How should investors think about share progression given the move from ~2 to ~4 and ~12 share in Florida?

Florida shows 'tons of growth left'; 2022 is fighting for one shelf, next year two; activating the 288-distributor network is the critical lever; passed Rockstar to #4, now targets passing Bang (#3) in the 'relatively near future' (no specific timing).
Velocity vs distribution points & Bang as proxy
Where is Celsius in the evolution of share moving into distribution points, and is Bang's trajectory a good proxy?
Already in many high-volume accounts (Circle K, 7-Eleven, CVS) with optimization runway; large untapped distribution (Walgreens, Dollar, Kroger banners); ~80% ACV is the sweet spot.
What drove velocity higher even as distribution expanded?

'Backdooring' the energy category - existing accounts converting to DSD (100%+ lift) plus new distribution added in the most productive convenience doors; Bang's 2018 success opened the channel's eyes to better-for-you brands.
How much of the velocity-driving consumer is new versus repeat, and how is it measured?
Business model could not work on new customers alone; high-continuity product, evidenced by sustained Amazon/Instacart momentum; loyal daily-routine consumer base.
How will retailers react to the (undisclosed) price increase, and will it go through?

Celsius has taken price for 52 weeks via ARP gains and promo roll-back with velocity still rising; confirmed an April 1 frontline increase, fully in by Q4 in a three-tier rollout; not 100% in numbers immediately due to annual contracts.
Was there a price-point threshold Celsius did not want to cross, and any elasticity thinking?
Deliberately avoided $2.99 and cannot price above Red Bull; targets between Monster and Red Bull (accounting for the 12oz vs 16oz size gap); $2.59-$2.79 is the desired convenience price point.
How much of the pre-list-price promotional pricing (~4%) gets given back, and is the list increase incremental?
Category pricing probably stays around 4-6%; the list increase is incremental to existing market pricing; will be blended in over time via promotional strategies.
Is the industry norm of roughly half the year on promotion the right 'sweet spot'?
Conceded it is an industry norm expected by retailers, not necessarily proven optimal, but necessary to compete and secure secondary placement; Celsius tests promotional mechanics to optimize profit.
At what revenue point does Celsius start to leverage into higher (peer) margins, and why could that number be large?

Significant margin opportunity and operating leverage left; deliberately over-investing ahead of revenue; benchmarks against Monster's ~$700-800M revenue inflection range with a similar product profile and business model.
